title: CAP Theorem & Practical Trade-offs
oneLiner: Distributed consensus principle stating a partitioned system must choose between Consistency and Availability.
imagePrompt: CAP triangle diagram highlighting CP vs AP trade-offs during network partition

body.definition: The CAP Theorem proves that a distributed data store can simultaneously provide at most two of three guarantees: Consistency (linearizability), Availability, and Partition Tolerance.
body.whyItMatters: Because network partitions (P) are unavoidable in physical networks, real systems must fundamentally choose between CP (rejecting writes/reads to preserve consistency) or AP (serving stale data for uptime).
body.commonPitfall: Treating CAP as picking any 2 of 3 (e.g., CA). Network partitions cannot be opted out of in distributed physical hardware.
body.interviewAngle: Evaluated when designing banking ledgers (CP required) vs social media feeds or shopping carts (AP with eventual consistency preferred).

quickChecks.question: Why is a 'CA' system impossible in distributed infrastructure?
quickChecks.answer: Network partitions (P) are physical realities that cannot be disabled.

quickChecks.question: What happens to an AP system during a network split?
quickChecks.answer: Both partitions continue serving reads and writes, resulting in divergent state.

title: Consistent Hashing & Ring Distribution
oneLiner: Hash distribution scheme minimizing key reassignment to k/n during cluster node scaling.
imagePrompt: Consistent hashing ring diagram with virtual nodes mapping request keys clockwise

body.definition: Consistent Hashing maps both cluster nodes and data keys onto a circular hash space (0 to 2^32-1), where keys route to the nearest clockwise node.
body.whyItMatters: When nodes are added or removed, only k/n keys must be migrated (where k = keys, n = nodes), unlike mod hashing (hash(key) % n) which causes 100% cache invalidation.
body.commonPitfall: Deploying without virtual nodes (vnodes), causing non-uniform key distribution and hot spots on neighboring physical servers.
body.interviewAngle: Core mechanism behind distributed caches (Memcached), distributed databases (DynamoDB, Cassandra), and load balancers.

quickChecks.question: What fraction of keys move when adding a node in a ring with n servers?
Why are virtual nodes (vnodes) essential in consistent hashing?
quickChecks.answer: They distribute hashing points uniformly around the ring to prevent data skew.

title: Rate Limiting (Token & Leaky Bucket)
oneLiner: Traffic shaping algorithms preventing service degradation, API abuse, and cascading failures.
imagePrompt: Token bucket refill rate vs capacity consuming tokens per incoming request

body.definition: Rate Limiting controls the rate of traffic sent or received by an endpoint, protecting backend compute and database resources from overload.
body.whyItMatters: Prevents DDoS attacks, brute-force exploits, noisy-neighbor starvation in multi-tenant environments, and upstream payment gateway quota exhaustion.
body.commonPitfall: Using naive Fixed Window counters that permit double the allowed quota across the window boundary threshold (e.g. 59s to 01s).
body.interviewAngle: Tested via API Gateway design, sliding window log counters in Redis using ZSETs, and handling HTTP 429 Too Many Requests.

quickChecks.question: What is the key advantage of Token Bucket over Leaky Bucket?
quickChecks.answer: Token Bucket allows controlled burst traffic up to bucket capacity.

quickChecks.question: How is distributed rate limiting implemented atomically in Redis?
quickChecks.answer: Using Redis Lua scripts or atomic pipeline token bucket updates.

title: CQRS & Event Sourcing Architecture
oneLiner: Architectural pattern separating read and write data models while capturing state as an append-only event log.
imagePrompt: CQRS architecture separating command write store and event bus projecting to read views

body.definition: Command Query Responsibility Segregation (CQRS) separates read and update operations for a data store, while Event Sourcing stores the state of a business entity as an append-only sequence of state-changing events.
body.whyItMatters: Enables independent scaling and optimization of read and write workloads, provides an immutable audit log, and allows rebuilding read models or temporal queries at any point in history.
body.commonPitfall: Assuming immediate consistency across read models. CQRS read projections are eventually consistent and must handle synchronization delays.
body.interviewAngle: Standard design pattern for financial transaction engines, e-commerce order workflows, and collaborative editing platforms.

quickChecks.question: What is the primary benefit of Event Sourcing for debugging and auditing?
quickChecks.answer: Complete immutable history of every state change allowing past replay.

quickChecks.question: How do read models stay updated in CQRS?
quickChecks.answer: Event handlers asynchronously subscribe to domain events and project state into read databases.

title: Circuit Breaker Pattern
oneLiner: Resilience pattern detecting distributed service failures and wrapping requests to prevent cascading downtime.
imagePrompt: State machine showing Closed, Open, and Half-Open circuit states

body.definition: A Circuit Breaker wraps network calls in a state machine (Closed, Open, Half-Open) that monitors failure rates and trips open to fast-fail subsequent requests when downstream services degrade.
body.whyItMatters: Stops cascading failures by preventing client threads and connection pools from blocking indefinitely on unresponsive downstream dependencies.
body.commonPitfall: Setting trip thresholds based on absolute failure counts instead of error percentages, causing false positives during traffic spikes.
body.interviewAngle: Evaluated in microservice reliability questions, fallback responses, and graceful degradation strategies under load.

quickChecks.question: What happens in the 'Half-Open' circuit state?
quickChecks.answer: A trial number of requests are permitted through to probe if downstream service recovered.

quickChecks.question: Why is fast-failing better than waiting for connection timeouts?
quickChecks.answer: It instantly frees application threads and prevents resource exhaustion.
